title: planner Review: A Solid Plan Template That Wants a Human in the Loop
description: We used am-will's planner skill to plan a real feature for our own site. The plan found existing code to reuse and a risk we had not spotted. The skill is built around asking you questions first, and it leans on a separate docs skill.

author.name: TrustedSkills Team
author.bio: We assess AI agent skills by installing them, running them against real work, and reading the source. We don't accept payment for reviews.

basisNote: Part of a batch of twelve developer-workflow skills run on the same day against the same codebase: the TrustedSkills website repo, a Next.js 16 app. Each run worked in its own private copy of the repo. One run on one codebase is one data point, not a benchmark.

runs.task: Plan a "Reviewed" filter for the site's skill browser, so a reader can list only skills with a hands-on review. Plan only; no code.
runs.outcome:
`npx skills add am-will/codex-skills --skill planner` installed it first time. The run took about six minutes.

The skill starts with research, then asks the user 5 to 10 clarifying questions before it writes anything. Nobody was there to answer, so the agent answered its own questions and recorded them. It then wrote a 278-line plan in the skill's template: three sprints, file-level tasks, acceptance criteria, a testing strategy, risks and a rollback plan. It saved it under the file name rule the skill gives.

We checked the plan's two key claims. The site already has a function that returns the set of reviewed skills, and the plan reuses it instead of adding new data code. And today that set is empty in a production build, because every hands-on review on disk is still a draft. The plan makes that its main risk and hides the new filter while the set is empty, so the site never shows a control that does nothing. Both are correct.

The skill's documentation step uses a separate Context7 skill. This feature needed no outside library docs, so that step was skipped, as the skill allows.
runs.environment: Claude Code subagent (Sonnet 5) with the installed SKILL.md loaded as its instructions, in a private clone of the TrustedSkills website repo at commit eca93fb. No Context7 skill installed.

summary: planner turns a feature request into a plan you could hand to someone: sprints that each end in something demoable, atomic tasks with file paths, and a rollback plan. On our repo the research step paid off: it found code to reuse and a real risk. Its weak points are the parts outside the template. It expects a person to answer questions, it relies on a separate docs skill, and it hasn't changed in eight months.

strengths.title: A template that forces the useful parts
strengths.body: Every sprint needs a demo and a check, and every task needs a file path, a dependency and a way to validate it. Plans written to it are hard to leave vague.

strengths.title: Research before writing
strengths.body: Phase 0 sends the agent into the codebase first. That is how it found the existing reviewed-skills function and the empty-set risk.

strengths.title: A second look after saving
strengths.body: The gotchas step, after the plan is saved, is a good habit. Here it turned up the difference between what development and production builds show.

limitations.title: Built for a live conversation
limitations.body: It stops to ask 5 to 10 questions before planning, and up to 3 more afterwards. That is right with a person present. Run unattended, the agent has to answer itself.

limitations.title: Depends on another skill
limitations.body: Phase 2 tells you to use the Context7 skill for library docs. It is not installed with planner, and the skill says nothing about what to do without it.

limitations.title: Small editing slips
limitations.body: Two different sections are both headed "Phase 3". It mentions a `request_user_input` tool that is not a Claude Code tool.

limitations.title: Not recently maintained
limitations.body: The skill's folder was last changed in January 2026.

bestFor.title: Planning a feature with a person on hand
bestFor.body: Answer its questions, and the template does the rest.

bestFor.title: Handing work to other agents
bestFor.body: Atomic tasks with dependencies are easy to split across parallel workers.

notFor: Small fixes. A three-sprint template around a one-line change is overhead.
